claim: The number of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles released into the synaptic cleft with each action potential dictates the reliability of synaptic transmission.
source: The number of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles released into the synaptic cleft with each action potential dictates the reliability of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claim: Variability in the number of vesicles released provides diversity of synaptic function across brain regions.
source: Variability of this fundamental property provides diversity of synaptic function across brain regions, but the source of this variability is unclear.
evidence: This statement draws on established understanding of synaptic diversity.

claim: The prevailing view is that release of a single or multiple vesicles reflects variability in vesicle release probability.
source: The prevailing view is that release of a single (univesicular release, UVR) or multiple vesicles (multivesicular release, MVR) reflects variability in vesicle release probability, a notion that is well-supported by the calcium-dependence of release mode.
evidence: This references existing scientific consensus in the field.

claim: The number of vesicles released is regulated by the size of the readily-releasable pool, upstream of vesicle release probability.
source: However, using mouse brain slices, we now demonstrate that the number of vesicles released is regulated by the size of the readily-releasable pool, upstream of vesicle release probability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Protein kinase A and synapsin dynamically control release site occupancy to dictate the number of vesicles released without altering release probability.
source: Our results point to a model wherein protein kinase A and its vesicle-associated target, synapsin, dynamically control release site occupancy to dictate the number of vesicles released without altering release probability.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Multiple vesicles can be released from a given active zone, a process termed multivesicular release (MVR).
source: Although the one-site-one-vesicle hypothesis was well accepted for decades, a wealth of evidence now demonstrates that multiple vesicles can be released from a given active zone, a process termed multivesicular release (MVR; Tong and Jahr, 1994; Auger et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MVR is widespread in the rodent CNS.
source: MVR is widespread in the rodent CNS and it appears to be the dominant release mode in human cortex (Rudolph et al., 2015; Molnár et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: MVR appears to be the dominant release mode in human cortex.
source: MVR is widespread in the rodent CNS and it appears to be the dominant release mode in human cortex (Rudolph et al., 2015; Molnár et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some synapses are limited to the release of a single vesicle per active zone (UVR).
source: Yet some synapses are limited to the release of a single vesicle per active zone, termed univesicular release (UVR; Korn et al., 1981; Stevens and Wang, 1995; Silver, 2003; Biró et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some synapses switch release modes in an activity-dependent manner.
source: and other synapses switch release modes in an activity-dependent manner (Bender et al., 2009; Higley et al., 2009; Pulido et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Forskolin increased the peak amplitude of CF-PC EPSCs by approximately 33%.
source: As in other synapses, the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (fsk; Figure 1A left) potentiated neurotransmitter release as measured by ~33% increase in the peak amplitude of EPSCs (Salin et al., 1996; Chen and Regehr, 1997; Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Bender et al., 2009; Cousin and Evans, 2011; Midorikawa and Sakaba, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and cited prior work.

claim: Forskolin-mediated increase of EPSCs was not accompanied by a change in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR).
source: However, the fsk-mediated increase of EPSCs was not accompanied by a change in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR; Figure 1A middle and right panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fsk increased the EPSC amplitude from 1.6 ± 0.2 nA to 2.1 ± 0.3 nA (p<0.0001).
source: Fsk increased the EPSC amplitude (from 1.6 ± 0.2 nA to 2.1 ± 0.3 nA; p<0.0001, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fsk did not change the PPR (from 1.1 ± 0.03 to 1.1 ± 0.05, n = 10 each; p=0.27).
source: without changing the PPR (from 1.1 ± 0.03 to 1.1 ± 0.05, n = 10 each; p=0.27).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 6-Bnz increased the EPSC amplitude from 0.6 ± 0.1 nA to 0.7 ± 0.1 nA (p=0.0009).
source: Likewise, 6-Bnz increased the EPSC amplitude (from 0.6 ± 0.1 nA to 0.7 ± 0.1 nA; p=0.0009, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 6-Bnz did not change the PPR (from 1.4 ± 0.07 to 1.4 ± 0.05, n = 10 each; p=0.68).
source: without changing the PPR (from 1.4 ± 0.07 to 1.4 ± 0.05, n = 10 each; p=0.68).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSCs was not altered by forskolin treatment (104.1 ± 44.9%; n = 5, p=0.93).
source: Consistent with a lack of change in Pr, the coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSCs was not altered by either fsk or 6-Bnz treatment (104.1 ± 44.9% and 101.9 ± 40.1%; n = 5 and 10, p=0.93 and 0.96, one sample t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSCs was not altered by 6-Bnz treatment (101.9 ± 40.1%; n = 10, p=0.96).
source: Consistent with a lack of change in Pr, the coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSCs was not altered by either fsk or 6-Bnz treatment (104.1 ± 44.9% and 101.9 ± 40.1%; n = 5 and 10, p=0.93 and 0.96, one sample t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: Reducing the amplitude of AMPAR-mediated EPSCs with NBQX resulted in a CV of 97.6 ± 38.3% (n = 4, p=0.95).
source: a similar result to reducing the amplitude of AMPA receptor (AMPAR)-mediated EPSCs with NBQX (97.6 ± 38.3%; n = 4, p=0.95).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: Altering Pr by manipulating extracellular Ca2+ robustly changed the CV (216.4 ± 27.6% and 49.2 ± 8.6%, respectively; p=0.01 and 0.03, n = 5 and 3).
source: In contrast, altering Pr by manipulating extracellular Ca2+, robustly changed the CV (216.4 ± 27.6% and 49.2 ± 8.6%, respectively; p=0.01 and 0.03, n = 5 and 3; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both forskolin and 6-Bnz reduced % EPSC inhibition by kynurenic acid.
source: Both fsk and 6-Bnz reduced % EPSC inhibition by kyn from 68.3 ± 1.5% in control (n = 11) to 36.5 ± 3.8% in fsk (n = 7; p<0.0001) and to 42.8 ± 3.3% in 6-Bnz (n = 7; p<0.0001; ANOVAs followed by Holm-Sidak post-tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neither forskolin nor 6-Bnz affected %EPSC inhibition by NBQX.
source: In contrast, neither fsk nor 6-Bnz affected %EPSC inhibition by NBQX (control: 40.7 ± 4.6%, n = 6; fsk: 42.7 ± 3.0%, n = 4, p=0.98; 6-Bnz: 36.6 ± 1.7%, n = 5; p=0.92, ANOVA).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increasing stimulation frequency between 0.1 and 20 Hz reduced EPSCs due to decrease in the number of active release sites.
source: Increasing stimulation frequency between 0.1 and 20 Hz reduced EPSCs due to decrease the number of active release sites, confirmed by variance/mean analysis (Foster and Regehr, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and cited prior work.

claim: Kynurenic acid (1 mM) inhibited EPSCs by 82.2 ± 0.9% at 0.1 Hz, 86.7 ± 1.2% at 1 Hz, 83.7 ± 2.8% at 2 Hz (n = 5 each; p=0.3).
source: The LAA, kynurenic acid (KYN; 1 mM), inhibited EPSCs by 82.2 ± 0.9% at 0.1 Hz, 86.7 ± 1.2% at 1 Hz, 83.7 ± 2.8% at 2 Hz; n = 5 each; p=0.3, ANOVA).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NBQX (100 nM) blocked EPSCs by 52.7 ± 1.8% at 0.1 Hz, 53.6 ± 1.9% at 1 Hz, 52.9 ± 2.4% at 2 Hz (n = 5 each; p=0.9).
source: The high-affinity antagonist NBQX (100 nM) that is insensitive to cleft glutamate concentration blocked EPSCs by 52.7 ± 1.8% at 0.1 Hz, 53.6 ± 1.9% at 1 Hz, 52.9 ± 2.4% at 2 Hz, n = 5 each; p=0.9, ANOVA).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Varying the number of active release sites does not influence the synaptic glutamate concentration.
source: Thus, varying the number of active release sites does not influence the synaptic glutamate concentration.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing consistent LAA inhibition across different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Forskolin and 6-Bnz markedly reduced KYN inhibition without affecting NBQX inhibition, suggesting that the average synaptic glutamate concentration is higher following stimulation of cAMP/PKA signaling.
source: We found that both activators markedly reduced KYN inhibition without affecting NBQX inhibition, strongly suggesting that the average synaptic glutamate concentration is higher following stimulation of cAMP/PKA signaling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Stimulation of the cAMP/PKA pathway increases the synaptic glutamate concentration without altering Pr.
source: Together these data show that stimulation of the cAMP/PKA pathway increases the synaptic glutamate concentration without altering Pr.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: 6-Bnz increased the frequency of asynchronous EPSCs from 1.3 ± 0.2 to 3.5 ± 0.8 Hz (n = 6, p=0.04).
source: 6-Bnz increased the frequency of aEPSCs (from 1.3 ± 0.2 to 3.5 ± 0.8 Hz; n = 6, p=0.04)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 6-Bnz had no effect on the average amplitude of asynchronous EPSCs (55 ± 4 pA and 56 ± 3 pA; n = 6, p=0.7).
source: 6-Bnz had no effect on the cumulative amplitude probability histogram, aEPSC average amplitude (55 ± 4 pA and 56 ± 3 pA; n = 6, p=0.7)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 6-Bnz had no effect on aEPSC kinetics (rise: 0.21 ± 0.02 ms and 0.22 ± 0.02 ms; decay: 1.8 ms ± 0.2 and 1.8 ms ± 0.2; n = 6, p=0.5).
source: or aEPSC kinetics (rise: 0.21 ± 0.02 ms and 0.22 ± 0.02 ms; decay: 1.8 ms ± 0.2 and 1.8 ms ± 0.2; n = 6, p=0.5; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PKA stimulation does not affect quantal size but may increase the total number of vesicles available for release.
source: demonstrating that PKA stimulation does not affect quantal size but, rather, may increase the total number of vesicles available for release.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the aEPSC data showing no change in amplitude but increased frequency.

claim: PKA activation enhanced the size of the RRP by approximately 30% (5.0 ± 0.9 nA and 6.7 ± 1.2 nA, n = 6, p=0.04).
source: Linear regression of the last EPSCs (see Materials and methods) showed that PKA activation enhanced the size of the RRP by ~30% (5.0 ± 0.9 nA and 6.7 ± 1.2 nA, n = 6, p=0.04)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PKA activation did not change Pr (calculated as the ratio of the initial EPSC to the y-intercept of the cumulative EPSC; 0.03 ± 0.005 and 0.03 ± 0.003, p=0.8).
source: without changing Pr (calculated as the ratio of the initial EPSC to the y-intercept of the cumulative EPSC; 0.03 ± 0.005 and 0.03 ± 0.003, p=0.8; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Stimulation of the cAMP/PKA pathway under UVR conditions (0.5 mM Ca2+) increased the synaptic glutamate concentration by increasing the size of the RRP rather than affecting Pr or quantal size.
source: These data show that stimulation of the cAMP/PKA pathway under UVR conditions (0.5 mM Ca2+) increased the synaptic glutamate concentration by increasing the size of the RRP rather than affecting Pr or quantal size.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Neither forskolin nor 6-Bnz altered EPSC amplitude in 2.5 mM Ca2+ (99 ± 2% and 100 ± 1% of control with fsk and 6-Bnz, respectively).
source: Surprisingly, neither fsk nor 6-Bnz application altered EPSC amplitude (99 ± 2% and 100 ± 1% of control with fsk and 6-Bnz, respectively)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neither forskolin nor 6-Bnz altered short-term plasticity in 2.5 mM Ca2+ (PPR = 0.15 ± 0.01, 0.17 ± 0.02 and 0.15 ± 0.03 in control, fsk and 6-Bnz, respectively, n = 12, 6, and 6).
source: or short-term plasticity (PPR = 0.15 ± 0.01, 0.17 ± 0.02 and 0.15 ± 0.03 in control, fsk and 6-Bnz, respectively, n = 12, 6, and 6; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: cAMP/PKA signaling does not further potentiate existing MVR.
source: Thus, cAMP/PKA signaling does not further potentiate existing MVR, suggesting that the effects of cAMP/PKA on vesicular release may be occluded when MVR is prevalent.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of effect of PKA activators in high Ca2+ conditions.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ can alter the size of the RRP.
source: Extracellular Ca2+ not only regulates Pr, but can also alter the size of the RRP (Schneggenburger et al., 1999; Thanawala and Regehr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In high Pr conditions (2.5 mM Ca2+) MVR is maximized by both an increase in Pr and an increase in the size of the RRP, thus occluding further effects of PKA activation.
source: We hypothesized that in high Pr conditions (2.5 mM Ca2+) MVR is maximized by both an increase in Pr and an increase the size of the RRP, thus occluding further effects of PKA activation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: KT5720 and Rp-8Br-cAMPs reduced MVR.
source: We tested this idea by preincubating slices in either KT5720 (1 µM), an active-site directed inhibitor that occupies PKA's ATP binding pocket and prevents phosphorylation of its substrates, or Rp-8Br-cAMPs (50 µM), a cAMP analog that prevents the dissociation of PKA's regulatory subunits from its catalytic subunits. Both compounds are expected to lower the effective PKA concentration at terminals, and indeed, both reduced MVR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased KYN inhibition.

claim: CF-PC EPSC inhibition by KYN (1 mM) in control was 26 ± 4% (n = 10) and was increased in slices pretreated with KT5720 or 8-Br-cAMPs (47 ± 3% and 42 ± 2%, n = 6 and 7, p=0.0004 and p=0.0048, respectively).
source: We found that CF-PC EPSC inhibition by KYN (1 mM) in control (26 ± 4%, n = 10) was increased in slices pretreated with KT5720- or 8-Br-cAMPs (47 ± 3% and 42 ± 2%, n = 6 and 7, p=0.0004 and p=0.0048, respectively; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: NBQX (100 nM) inhibition was similar with all treatments (control: 34 ± 3%, KT5720: 33 ± 2%, 8-Br-cAMPs: 33 ± 5%; n = 9, 4, and 3, p=0.97).
source: In contrast, NBQX (100 nM) inhibition was similar with all treatments (control: 34 ± 3%, KT5720: 33 ± 2%, 8-Br-cAMPs: 33 ± 5%; n = 9, 4, and 3, p=0.97; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reduction in MVR did not result from reduced Pr.
source: Consistent with our results shown above, the reduction in MVR did not result from reduced Pr, which we measured with two methods.
evidence: This conclusion is based on PPR and PPD measurements.

claim: PKA-mediated changes in MVR are independent from Pr, since neither KT5720 nor 8-Br-cAMPs altered estimates of Pr.
source: Together, these data suggest that PKA-mediated changes in MVR are independent from Pr, since neither KT5720 nor 8-Br-cAMPs altered these widely-used estimates of Pr.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing no change in PPR with PKA inhibition.

claim: cAMP/PKA stimulation increased release only under low extracellular Ca2+, whereas the effects of cAMP/PKA activation were occluded in elevated Ca2+.
source: Interestingly, we found that cAMP/PKA stimulation increased release only under low extracellular Ca2+ whereas, the effects of cAMP/PKA activation were occluded in elevated Ca2+.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations.

claim: Robust Ca2+ influx is sufficient to stimulate adenylyl cyclases (ACs) to generate cAMP.
source: It is well known that robust Ca2+ influx is sufficient to stimulate adenylyl cyclases (ACs) to generate cAMP (Salin et al., 1996; Wong et al., 1999; Moulder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Sufficient Ca2+ influx in 2.5 mM extracellular Ca2+ may allow stimulation of the cAMP/PKA pathway at CF synapses.
source: Sufficient Ca2+ influx in 2.5 mM extracellular Ca2+ may thus allow stimulation of this pathway at CF synapses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of Ca2+ and adenylyl cyclases.

claim: The Ca2+ dependence of cAMP/PKA-synapsin signaling at CF synapses contributes to the basal size of the RRP that is known to change in response to extracellular Ca2+.
source: We speculate that the Ca2+ dependence of cAMP/PKA-synapsin signaling at CF synapses contributes to the basal size of the RRP that is known to change in response to extracellular Ca2+ (compare Figures 2 and 5; Schneggenburger et al., 1999; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Thanawala and Regehr, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on experimental observations and cited prior work.

claim: KT5720 caused a 43% increase in KYN's ability to inhibit EPSCs at the highest Ca2+ concentration tested (64.7 ± 5.1%, n = 4 and 36.2 ± 4.9%, n = 5; in KT5720 and control, respectively).
source: KT5720 did cause a 43% increase in KYN's ability to inhibit EPSCs at the highest Ca2+ concentration tested (64.7 ± 5.1%, n = 4 and 36.2 ± 4.9%, n = 5; in KT5720 and control, respectively; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Raising extracellular Ca2+ causes a PKA-mediated increase in the number of vesicles released that is independent of the expected Ca2+-mediated change in Pr.
source: This indicates that raising extracellular Ca2+ causes a PKA-mediated increase in the number of vesicles released that is independent of the expected Ca2+-mediated change in Pr.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing KT5720 effects on KYN inhibition.

claim: 57% of MVR results from changes in Pr whereas 43% of MVR is under the direct control of PKA activity.
source: These results suggest that MVR is controlled by two Ca2+-dependent processes: 57% of MVR results from changes in Pr whereas 43% of MVR is under the direct control of PKA activity (Figure 4D right).
evidence: This is a quantitative conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of PKA had no effect on the size or kinetics of Sr2+ evoked aEPSCs but reduced their frequency.
source: As an additional control, we found that inhibition of PKA with KT5720 had no effect on the size or kinetics of Sr2+ evoked aEPSCs but reduced their frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: PKA signaling modulates MVR by controlling the number of vesicles available for release that may be part of the RRP.
source: Together, bi-directional regulation of the glutamate concentration transient (Figure 1 and Figure 4) and of the aEPSC frequency (Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3) suggests that PKA signaling modulates MVR by controlling the number of vesicles available for release that may be part of the RRP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: PKA inhibition reduced the RRP to approximately half of that in control.
source: This estimate of the RRP (RRP train) showed that PKA inhibition reduced the RRP to approximately half of that in control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Neither Prtrain nor PrEQ differed significantly between control and KT5720-treated slices.
source: Consistent with estimates of Pr derived from PPD, neither Prtrain nor PrEQ differed significantly between control and KT5720-treated slices.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PKA activity alters the number of vesicles released per active zone independent of the likelihood that a release-competent vesicle fuses with the presynaptic membrane.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that PKA activity alters the number of vesicles released per active zone independent of the likelihood that a release-competent vesicle fuses with the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: PKA activity changes the RRP without altering Pr.
source: In other words, PKA activity changes the RRP without altering Pr.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: The A-domain of synapsin is an excellent PKA substrate that is well-known to regulate transmitter release.
source: Among the many presynaptic proteins that can be directly or indirectly regulated by PKA (Sudhof, 2004), the A-domain of synapsin is an excellent PKA substrate that is well-known to regulate transmitter release (Hosaka et al., 1999; Hilfiker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Complete loss of synapsin I, II and III does not alter transmission evoked by single stimuli but rather alters the rate of depression during repetitive stimulation.
source: At excitatory synapses, they are typically associated with regulation of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles because complete loss of synapsin I, II and III does not alter transmission evoked by single stimuli but rather alters the rate of depression during repetitive stimulation (Gitler et al., 2004a; Gitler et al., 2004b; Gitler et al., 2008; Vasileva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synapsin-dependent regulation of the RRP has been documented at inhibitory synapses.
source: Synapsin-dependent regulation of the RRP has been documented at inhibitory synapses (Baldelli et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: CF-PC EPSCs from het and TKO mice had similar kinetics, short-term plasticity, and recovered from depression with a time course similar to their wildtype counterparts.
source: In 2.5 mM Ca2+, CF-PC EPSCs from het and TKO mice had similar kinetics, short-term plasticity, and recovered from depression with a time course similar to their wildtype counterparts (data not shown and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Estimates of Pr at 10 ms ISI were similar to that in wildtype recordings (0.92 ± 0.01 and 0.93 ± 0.01 at 10 ms ISI, n = 10 and 8, p=0.4).
source: Our estimates of Pr at 10 ms ISI, when little replenishment is assumed to have taken place, were similar to that in wildtype recordings (0.92 ± 0.01 and 0.93 ± 0.01 at 10 ms ISI, n = 10 and 8, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: Peak EPSC amplitudes from TKO mice were 45% smaller compared to their het littermates (het: 13.5 ± 0.98 nA; TKO: 7.8 ± 0.59 nA, n = 6 each, p=0006).
source: However, peak EPSC amplitudes from TKO mice were 45% smaller compared to their het littermates (het: 13.5 ± 0.98 nA; TKO: 7.8 ± 0.59 nA, n = 6 each, p=0006).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: The RRP from TKO mice was about half the size as in het littermates without a change in estimated Pr.
source: We estimated the size of the RRP and found that, on average, the RRP from TKO mice was about half the size as in het littermates without a change in estimated Pr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurotransmitter release in TKO mice mimics inhibition of PKA signaling: reduced RRP with no change in Pr.
source: Together these results show that neurotransmitter release in TKO mice mimics inhibition of PKA signaling: reduced RRP with no change in Pr (compare with Figure 4C and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data comparing TKO mice to PKA inhibition.

claim: 6-Bnz potentiated EPSCs in het mice by 34% (from 0.91 ± 0.12 nA to 1.22 ± 16 nA, n = 7, p=0.008) without a change in PPR (from 1.46 ± 0.07 to 1.42 ± 0.06, p=0.54).
source: First, we recorded in low Pr conditions, when UVR predominates (0.5 mM Ca2+), and showed that 6-Bnz potentiated EPSCs in het mice by 34% (from 0.91 ± 0.12 nA to 1.22 ± 16 nA, n = 7, p=0.008, paired t-test) without a change in PPR (Figure 6Ai; from 1.46 ± 0.07 to 1.42 ± 0.06, p=0.54)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 6Ai.

claim: 6-Bnz had no effect on either the amplitude or PPR of CF-EPSCs in TKO mice.
source: However, 6-Bnz had no effect on either the amplitude or PPR of CF-EPSCs in TKO mice (Figure 6Aii).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6Aii.

claim: EPSCs enhanced by Bnz-cAMP in het mice exhibited reduced inhibition by KYN whereas KYN inhibition was unchanged by 6-Bnz in TKO littermates.
source: Consistent with wildtype mice (Figure 1), EPSCs enhanced by Bnz-cAMP in het mice exhibited reduced inhibition by KYN whereas KYN inhibition was unchanged by 6-Bnz in TKO littermates (Figure 6Bi).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6Bi.

claim: PKA-induced MVR was absent in synapsin TKO mice.
source: Thus, PKA-induced MVR was absent in synapsin TKO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in TKO mice.

claim: KT5720 increased KYN (1 mM) block in het slices (control: 27.6 ± 4.0% and KT5720: 43.2 ± 2.7, n = 6 and 7, p=0.02), but there was no difference in KYN block in slices from TKO mice (control: 41.8 ± 2.5% and KT5720: 41.8 ± 2.9%, n = 6 each; p=0.99).
source: KT5720 increased the KYN (1 mM) block in het slices (control: 27.6 ± 4.0% and KT5720: 43.2 ± 2.7, n = 6 and 7, p=0.02), but there was no difference in KYN block in slices from TKO mice (control: 41.8 ± 2.5% and KT5720: 41.8 ± 2.9%, n = 6 each; p=0.99, 2-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 6Ci and Cii.

claim: Suppression of MVR by PKA inhibition was absent in synapsin TKO mice.
source: Thus, suppression of MVR by PKA inhibition was absent in synapsin TKO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in TKO mice.

claim: Synapsins may be the principal targets of PKA at CF synapses.
source: Altogether these data suggest that synapsins may be the principal targets of PKA at CF synapses and that this family of proteins is required for bidirectional regulation of MVR via regulation of the RRP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in TKO mice.

claim: Synapsins are required for bidirectional regulation of MVR via regulation of the RRP.
source: Altogether these data suggest that synapsins may be the principal targets of PKA at CF synapses and that this family of proteins is required for bidirectional regulation of MVR via regulation of the RRP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in TKO mice.

claim: PKA-dependent regulation of the RRP bidirectionally transforms the release mode at CF synapses (UVR ⇔ MVR) without affecting Pr.
source: Our results show PKA-dependent regulation of the RRP bidirectionally transforms the release mode at CF synapses (UVR ⇔ MVR) without affecting Pr.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental results.

claim: The RRP is a functional measure of the number of release-competent vesicles per active zone, that is under the control of synapsins, and constrains the number of vesicles released (MVR).
source: The simplest explanation for our results is that the RRP is a functional measure of the number of release-competent vesicles per active zone, that is under the control of synapsins, and constrains the number of vesicles released (MVR).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental results.

claim: A model that incorporates PKA-mediated control of the RRP is sufficient to recapitulate experimental results and reconcile those at other synapses.
source: Thus, a model that incorporates PKA-mediated control of the RRP is sufficient to recapitulate our experimental results and reconcile those at other synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: High Pr is not required for MVR at CF synapses where this release mode predominates.
source: These results show that PKA-mediated regulation of RRP is sufficient to generate a bi-directional shift in release mode (from MVR→UVR or UVR→MVR) without changing Psucc, thus illustrating that high Pr is not required for MVR at CF synapses where this release mode predominates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on modeling and experimental results.

claim: Approximately 25% of PF synapses can alter release mode from UVR to MVR in response to potentiation of cAMP/PKA signaling.
source: This suggests that approximately 25% of PF synapses can alter release mode from UVR to MVR in response to potentiation of cAMP/PKA signaling (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a quantitative conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: cAMP/PKA signaling can enhance MVR without altering Pr at PF synapses as well as CF synapses.
source: Altogether these results show that cAMP/PKA signaling can enhance MVR without altering Pr at PF synapses as well as CF synapses, and that this signaling pathway can also facilitate presynaptic function by enhancing Pr at PF synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in PF synapses.

claim: cAMP/PKA signaling primarily elevates MVR via regulation of the RRP.
source: Since PF synapses with fsk-induced enhanced Pr did not display MVR, we conclude that cAMP/PKA signaling primarily elevates MVR via regulation of the RRP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in PF synapses.

claim: The number of glutamate-filled vesicles released at individual CF terminals with each action potential is subject to bidirectional modification of the RRP.
source: Our results show that the number of glutamate-filled vesicles released at individual CF terminals with each action potential is subject to bidirectional modification of the RRP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Altered cAMP/PKA activity changed the EPSC inhibition by a LAA, indicating a change in the synaptic glutamate concentration and thus the number of vesicles released per active zone.
source: Altered cAMP/PKA activity changed the EPSC inhibition by a LAA, a result that indicates a change in the synaptic glutamate concentration and thus the number of vesicles released per active zone.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Changes in cAMP/PKA activity did not affect Pr, as quantified by four separate measures, but rather altered the size of the RRP.
source: Surprisingly, changes in cAMP/PKA activity did not affect Pr, as quantified by four separate measures, but rather altered the size of the RRP.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: PKA-dependent signaling can shift the balance between MVR and UVR, but is maximally active in 2.5 mM Ca2+ at CFs.
source: We found that PKA-dependent signaling can shift the balance between MVR and UVR, but is maximally active in 2.5 mM Ca2+ at CFs.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Regulation of release mode by PKA requires synapsins.
source: Furthermore, regulation of release mode by PKA requires synapsins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in TKO mice.

claim: Release site occupancy or vesicle competency depend on the size of the RRP, upstream of Pr.
source: Our data is explained by a model where release site occupancy or vesicle competency depend on the size of the RRP, upstream of Pr.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental results.

claim: The original hypothesis that Pr exclusively dictates the propensity for MVR makes two assumptions: (1) that each active zone contains multiple docking sites, and (2) that each docking site is filled at rest.
source: The original hypothesis that Pr exclusively dictates the propensity for MVR makes two assumptions: (1) that each active zone contains multiple docking sites, and (2) that each docking site (sometimes referred to as a release site) is filled at rest, thus holding a primed vesicle that is competent for release.
evidence: This describes the prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: Each active zone contains multiple docking sites.
source: Together with prior studies, our results support the assumption that each active zone contains multiple docking sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental results and prior studies.

claim: Many studies provide converging evidence against the assumption that every release site is occupied at rest.
source: However, many studies provide converging evidence against the second assumption that every release site is occupied at rest and the analogous assumption that an anatomically-defined docked vesicle is release competent.
evidence: This references existing scientific literature.

claim: Factors beyond Pr must also contribute to MVR.
source: Evidence against the second assumption argues that factors beyond Pr must also contribute to MVR.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the evidence against the second assumption.

claim: A model that explains the propensity for MVR at low Pr synapses and UVR at high Pr synapses incorporates static docking site number with dynamic docking site occupancy and vesicle release probability.
source: We propose a model that explains the propensity for MVR at low Pr synapses and UVR at high Pr synapses by incorporating static docking site number with dynamic docking site occupancy and vesicle release probability.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental results.

claim: CFs have seven docking sites per active zone based on anatomically-defined docked vesicles.
source: We have modeled CFs as having seven docking sites per active zone based on anatomically-defined docked vesicles (Xu-Friedman et al., 2001)
evidence: This is based on a citation to a prior anatomical study.

claim: Data from synapsin-TKO shows no difference in the number of docked vesicles.
source: While it would be functionally equivalent for the number of active docking sites to serve as the dynamic variable with a constant occupancy, data from synapsin-TKO shows no difference in the number of docked vesicles (Gitler et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a prior study.

claim: The probability of CF docking/release site occupancy is approximately 0.7.
source: If we consider CFs that have 300 active zones (Llinas et al., 1969); and thus ~2100 sites), the probability of CF docking/release site occupancy is ~0.7, calculated from an estimate of 1400 functional docking sites (Foster and Regehr, 2004).
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited prior studies.

claim: Altering docking site occupancy is sufficient to shift the number of vesicles released per active zone without changing Pr (Psucc).
source: As shown in Figure 7C, altering docking site occupancy is sufficient to shift the number of vesicles released per active zone without changing Pr (Psucc), replicating our experimental data.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on modeling results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Activation of the cAMP cascade can alter synaptic transmission at PF-PC synapses by increasing the conductance of GluA3-containing AMPARs.
source: Activation of the cAMP cascade can alter synaptic transmission at PF-PC synapses by increasing the conductance of GluA3-containing AMPARs (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017) but see Chen and Regehr (1997).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Several lines of evidence argue against the possibility that PKA modulates AMPAR function.
source: Though our initial finding that activation of cAMP/PKA enhanced EPSC amplitude without changes in short-term plasticity or CV is consistent with modulation of AMPAR function, several lines of evidence argue against the possibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Neither activation nor inhibition of PKA altered the amplitude or kinetics of quantal-like aEPSCs.
source: First, neither activation nor inhibition of PKA altered the amplitude or kinetics of quantal-like aEPSCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Bath application of a PKA activator potentiated EPSCs even when a PKA inhibitory peptide was included in the pipette solution.
source: Second, bath application of a PKA activator potentiated EPSCs even when a PKA inhibitory peptide was included in the pipette solution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The effects of PKA activation were dependent on the external [Ca2+], as expected for a presynaptic process.
source: Third, the effects of PKA activation were dependent on the external [Ca2+], as expected for a presynaptic process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PKA modulation was associated with changes in the block by a LAA.
source: Fourth, PKA modulation was associated with changes in the block by a LAA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Activation of cAMP signaling did not enhance synaptic transmission in Synapsin TKOs.
source: Finally, activation of cAMP signaling did not enhance synaptic transmission in Synapsin TKOs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Modulation of the RRP, and not AMPARs, mediate the effects of PKA.
source: Taken together, these findings argue that modulation of the RRP, and not AMPARs, mediate the effects of PKA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Synapsins were initially proposed to control transitions of synaptic vesicles from the reserve pool to the RRP through phosphorylation-dependent interactions with actin.
source: Synapsins were initially proposed to control transitions of synaptic vesicles from the reserve pool to the RRP through phosphorylation-dependent interactions with actin (Greengard et al., 1993; Ceccaldi et al., 1995; Hosaka et al., 1999; Chi et al., 2001)
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Synapsins were later shown to be fundamental to post-docking steps of exocytosis.
source: and were later shown to be fundamental to post-docking steps of exocytosis (Rosahl et al., 1995; Hilfiker et al., 1998; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: A consensus view of synapsins' role in synaptic transmission may be hampered by subtype redundancy and potential for cell-type specific functions.
source: Although synapsins constitute one of the most abundant (Wilhelm et al., 2014) and highly studied families of presynaptic proteins, a consensus view of their role in synaptic transmission may be hampered by subtype redundancy and potential for cell-type specific functions (for example see Gitler et al., 2004a; Song and Augustine, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: Ca2+-dependent ACs and PKA may be compartmentalized in distinct subcellular domains providing additional mechanisms to regulate the Ca2+ sensitivity of this pathway.
source: Ca2+-dependent ACs and PKA may also be compartmentalized in distinct subcellular domains providing additional mechanisms to regulate the Ca2+ sensitivity of this pathway (Steinberg and Brunton, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited prior work.

claim: The Ca2+ dependence of cAMP/PKA-synapsin signaling at CF synapses contributes to the basal size of the RRP.
source: We speculate that the Ca2+ dependence of cAMP/PKA-synapsin signaling at CF synapses contributes to the basal size of the RRP that is known to change in response to extracellular Ca2+ (compare Figures 2 and 5; Schneggenburger et al., 1999; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Thanawala and Regehr, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on experimental observations and cited prior work.

claim: Diversity in Ca2+ homeostasis, ACs and PKA may contribute to the variability in PKA and synapsin-dependent regulation of release across synapses.
source: Diversity in Ca2+ homeostasis, ACs and PKA may thus contribute to the variability in PKA and synapsin-dependent regulation of release across synapses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Recent release models have proposed that vesicles transition between sequential states: from loose to tighter tethering with release machinery followed by Ca2+-triggered fusion.
source: Recent release models have proposed that vesicles transition between sequential states: from loose to tighter tethering with release machinery followed by Ca2+-triggered fusion (Neher and Brose, 2018)
evidence: This is based on a citation to a prior study.

claim: Estimates of release probability include the equilibrium between states.
source: These transitions are likely regulated by intracellular Ca2+ and thus, may occur too rapidly to discriminate using electrophysiological methods (Neher and Brose, 2018). Therefore, estimates of release probability include the equilibrium between states.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on cited prior work.

claim: Molecules such as synapsins contribute to the molecular machinery upstream of vesicle state transitions.
source: Our results support these models, assuming that molecules such as synapsins contribute to the molecular machinery upstream of these transitions, since PKA-dependent synapsin signaling changes the size of the RRP without affecting the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental results.

claim: Synapsin was proposed to form a distinct liquid phase that captures synaptic vesicles and is rapidly disassembled upon phosphorylation by CamKII.
source: Recently, synapsin was proposed to form a distinct liquid phase that captures synaptic vesicles and is rapidly disassembled upon phosphorylation by CamKII (Milovanovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a prior study.

claim: PKA phosphorylation triggers a mechanism similar to CamKII that allows vesicles to enter the loose/replacement sites.
source: We speculate that PKA phosphorylation triggers a similar mechanism that allows vesicles to enter the loose/replacement sites.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited prior work and experimental results.
